place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 山门 · 石壁
place.en: Chending Temple · The gate · the stone wall

setup.zh: 二试，脑子：一面石壁，刻着九个空格，一堆刻了数的石块。「横竖斜，加起来都要一样。」
setup.en: Second trial, wits: a stone wall carved with nine empty squares, a heap of numbered stones. "Across, down, corner to corner — they all add up the same."

recap.zh: 二试，洛书九宫：你想起娘教的口诀，「五居中央」。隔壁的石蛋把石头吞了：「吞了，就不算错。」
recap.en: Second trial, the Luo square: you remembered your mother's rhyme, "five in the centre". At the next wall Shidan swallowed his stones: "If I swallow them, it isn't wrong."

en: A stone wall, nine empty squares.
"Across, down, corner to corner — all the same."

story.zh:
一试下来，站在石阶顶上的，不过四五百人。送考的家里人，这时候也许从山侧一条小路绕上来，在山门外头等着。二试考脑子，在山门里头的一片石坪上。石坪上立着几十面石壁，每面石壁上刻着九个空格，横三竖三，像一张棋盘；石壁底下堆着九块石头，每块刻一个数，从一到九。一个管二试的老执事，背着手在石壁前走来走去，道：「横着加，竖着加，斜着加，都要一样。一炷香。」

有人把石头摆成了一朵花，有人摞成了一座塔，有人两块两块地换来换去，换了半炷香，越换越乱，把自己换哭了。小满隔壁那面石壁底下蹲的是石蛋。他盯着那九块石头看了很久很久，一块也没摆，然后把两块塞进了嘴里，第三块塞不进去，鼓着腮帮子还在往里按。老执事走过去，在他背上一拍，「噗噗」，两块石头吐了一地。旁边一个执事笑道：「每三年都有一个。」石蛋没笑，抹了一把嘴，红着眼睛道：「吞了，就不算错。」老执事看了他一会儿，没有说话，叹了口气，走开了。

小满听见了那句话。他想起他爹在路口说的：考不上，别回来。

石坪边上，隔开山门里外的，是一道矮墙。墙头上探着两颗脑袋，一颗是马家的家丁，一颗是葛六。葛六伸出指头来比划：先四根，再九根，再两根，一排一排地比，比得又快又稳，像镖局里对暗号。马小宝蹲在石壁底下，一面嚼桂花糕，一面照着比划摆石头。香才烧下去一小截，他已经拍拍手站了起来。横着加，十五；竖着加，十五；斜着加，还是十五。他摆完了，特地踱到小满跟前，伸着脖子看了一眼，鼻子里哼出三个字：「小意思。」

他娘是教过的。娘管这叫洛书，说是古时候洛水里出来的九个数：「戴九履一，左三右七，二四为肩，六八为足，五居中央。」小满照着摆：五搁在正当中，头顶九，脚下一，左手三，右手七。摆到两个肩膀，他记得娘念「二」的时候伸的是左手，便把二搁在左肩，四搁在右肩。一加，左边那一竖，二加三才五，要凑十五，脚底下得有一块十。九块石头里，没有十。铜炉里那炷香，已经烧过了一半。

墙头上，葛六的手指头还在比划，比给马小宝看的，小满也看得见：四，九，二。照着摆，一炷香都用不了。小满盯着那几根指头看了一会儿，把眼睛挪开了。马家的银子买来的东西，对，是马家的；错了，是一起死。他没有五两银子，也不想欠马家一个格子。可那几根手指头，倒叫他看出了一样东西：葛六冲着马小宝比划，站在墙那头，他的左手，是马小宝的右手。
story.en:
After the first trial, those standing at the top of the stair were no more than four or five hundred. The families who'd brought them were allowed up now by a path round the side of the mountain, to wait outside the gate. The second trial tested the head, on a stone terrace inside the gate. Dozens of stone walls stood on it, each carved with nine empty squares, three across and three down, like a game board; under each lay nine stones, each carved with a number from one to nine. The old steward in charge of the second trial paced before the walls, hands behind his back. "Add across, add down, add corner to corner — all the same. One stick of incense."

Some arranged the stones into a flower, some stacked them into a pagoda, some swapped them two by two for half a stick of incense, the more they swapped the worse it got, till they swapped themselves into tears. At the wall next to Xiaoman's squatted Shidan. He stared at the nine stones a long, long while, placed not one, and then put two into his mouth; the third wouldn't go in, and he was still pressing at it with his cheeks bulging. The old steward came over and clapped him on the back — *pff, pff* — and two stones landed on the ground. A steward nearby laughed: "Every three years there's one." Shidan didn't laugh. He wiped his mouth and said, red-eyed, "If I swallow them, it isn't wrong." The old steward looked at him a moment, said nothing, sighed, and walked away.

Xiaoman heard it. He thought of what the father had said on the flats: don't get in, don't come back.

At the edge of the terrace, dividing inside the gate from outside, was a low wall. Over the top of it peeped two heads — one a Ma servant's, one Ge Liu's. Ge Liu was signing with his fingers: four, then nine, then two, row after row, fast and steady, like a caravan's secret signal. Ma Xiaobao squatted at the foot of his wall, chewing osmanthus cake and setting stones by the signs. The incense had burned down only a little when he dusted his hands and stood. Across: fifteen; down: fifteen; corner to corner: fifteen again. Done, he strolled over to Xiaoman on purpose, craned his neck for a look, and snorted three words through his nose: "Easy as pie."

His mother had. She called it the Luo Shu, nine numbers that came out of the Luo River long ago: "Wear nine, tread one; three on the left, seven on the right; two and four for shoulders, six and eight for feet; five in the middle." Xiaoman set the stones by it: five in the middle, nine on the head, one under foot, three at the left hand, seven at the right. At the shoulders he remembered his mother reaching out her left hand as she said "two", so he put two at the left shoulder and four at the right. He added: down the left, two and three made only five; to make fifteen there would have to be a ten underfoot. Among nine stones there was no ten. The incense in the burner had burned past half.

On the wall Ge Liu's fingers were still signing — signing for Ma Xiaobao, but Xiaoman could see them too: four, nine, two. Copy them, and it wouldn't take a stick of incense. Xiaoman watched those fingers a moment, and looked away. What Ma silver bought, if it was right, was the Mas'; if it was wrong, you went down together. He had no five taels, and didn't want to owe the Mas a single square. But the fingers did show him one thing: Ge Liu was signing toward Ma Xiaobao, from the far side of the wall — his left hand was Ma Xiaobao's right.

exits.means: hands in the solved square, or asks to go on to the third trial

refuse.zh: 九宫还没填满。瞿老不看半张卷子。
refuse.en: The square is not filled yet. Elder Qu does not look at half an answer.

story.zh:
小满闭上眼睛。是那一夜的炕桌，娘也是坐在他对面，一颗一颗挪栗子。「左三右七」是嘴里念的，他照自己的左右摆，没错；「二」是看娘的手记的——娘伸的是娘的左手，娘坐在对面，娘的左手，落在他这边，是右。他把两个肩膀对调过来，二搁右，四搁左：横着加，十五；竖着加，十五；斜着加，十五。炉里的香，还剩一小截。

老执事先踱到马小宝那面石壁前，看了一会儿，点点头，问道：「五为什么在中间？」马小宝张了张嘴，眼睛往墙头上溜。老执事顺着他的眼睛往墙头上一看，看见了葛六，眉毛一挑：「葛六？」墙头上那颗脑袋「嗖」地缩了回去。老执事道：「二十年前，你那个『五』，也是背的。」他在马小宝的考牌上画了一笔——画的不是一道，是一个圈。

老执事又踱到小满跟前，问的还是那一句：「五为什么在中间？」小满道：「一配九，二配八，三配七，四配六，一对都是十，隔着中间那块，两头相望。九块石头，配剩下的，就是五。」老执事半天没说话，末了道：「谁教你的？」小满道：「口诀是我娘教的。为什么，是我方才算的。」

老执事「嗯」了一声，在他考牌上画了一道，却没有走，在石壁跟前一块石头上坐了下来，捶着腰道：「后人说，禹治水的时候得了这九个数，照着这九个格子，把天下分成了九州，又收了九州的铜，铸了九口鼎，一州一口。周朝不行了，鼎就没了——有人说，是沉在了山底下这条泗水里。秦始皇路过这里，发了一千个人下水去捞，《史记》上就两个字：弗得。本观开山的祖师，便在这山上结了庐，守着这条河，说德到了，鼎自己会浮起来。」说到这里，他顿了一顿，朝身后那座山看了一眼，声音低了些，「——这都是老辈子的话了。你娘教得好。你算得也好。」

小满把「九口鼎」三个字在嘴里嚼了一遍。他觉得胸口那块木牌好像动了一下，伸手去摸，却是凉的。

他转过身，石坪那一头，另一面石壁前，早有人摆好了——红鼻头，两根小辫子，蹲在石壁底下，拿炭条在一个蓝布面的小本子上低头记着什么。是阿禾。小满喊了一声，往那边挤了两步，人群一涌，再抬头看时，那石壁底下已经空了，只地上留着一截用秃了的炭条头。她是在躲他。

隔壁石壁底下，石蛋还蹲着，九块石头吐出来又摆回去，摆得歪歪扭扭，五搁在了边上。他的考牌上，只有石阶那一道。
story.en:
Xiaoman closed his eyes. It was the kang table that night: his mother sitting opposite him then too, moving chestnuts one by one. "Three on the left, seven on the right" was said aloud, and he'd placed them by his own left and right — that was fine. But "two" he'd remembered from her hand — she'd held up her left hand, and she was sitting across from him; her left, on his side, was right. He swapped the two shoulders: two on the right, four on the left. Across: fifteen; down: fifteen; corner to corner: fifteen. A little stub of incense was left in the burner.

The old steward went first to Ma Xiaobao's wall, looked a while, nodded, and asked: "Why is the five in the middle?" Ma Xiaobao opened his mouth, and his eyes slid toward the top of the wall. The old steward followed his eyes up the wall, saw Ge Liu, and raised a brow. "Ge Liu?" The head on the wall vanished with a whoosh. The old steward said, "Twenty years ago your 'five' was learned by rote too." He made a mark on Ma Xiaobao's tag — not a stroke, but a circle.

Then he came to Xiaoman and asked the same: "Why is the five in the middle?" Xiaoman said, "One pairs with nine, two with eight, three with seven, four with six — each pair makes ten, and they face each other across the middle stone. Of nine stones, the one left over after the pairing is five." The old steward said nothing for a long while, then: "Who taught you?" Xiaoman said, "The rhyme my mother taught me. The why, I just worked out."

The old steward said "Mm," and drew a stroke on his tag, but didn't move on; he sat down on a stone by the wall and thumped his back. "Those who came after say that when Yu tamed the floods he was given these nine numbers, and by these nine squares he divided the world into nine provinces, and gathered the bronze of the nine provinces and cast nine *ding* cauldrons, one to a province. When the Zhou declined, the *ding* were lost — some say they sank in the Si, the river under this very mountain. The First Emperor of Qin passed this way and sent a thousand men into the water to dredge for them; the *Records of the Grand Historian* give it two words: not found. The founder of this temple built a hut on this mountain to keep watch over the river, and said that when virtue arrived, the *ding* would float up of itself." Here he paused, glanced back at the mountain behind him, and lowered his voice. "— That's old folks' talk now. Your mother taught you well. And you reckoned well."

Xiaoman chewed the words "nine cauldrons" over once in his mouth. He thought the wooden token on his chest stirred, and reached for it; it was cold.

He turned. At the far end of the terrace, before another wall, someone had long finished — red nose, two little braids, squatting at the foot of the wall, writing something with charcoal in a little blue cloth-covered book, head down. Ah He. Xiaoman called out and pushed two steps toward her; the crowd surged, and when he looked again the foot of the wall was empty, only a worn-down stub of charcoal left on the ground. She was avoiding him.

At the next wall, Shidan was still squatting, spitting the nine stones out and putting them back, crooked, the five pushed to one side. On his tag there was only the one stroke from the stair.
